(i) aminogly-cosides do not improve the clinical efficacy of beta-lactam monotherapy in the treatment of bacteraemia, (ii) the use of aminogylcoside-containing regimens is associated with an increased risk of renal toxicity, and (iii) there is no association between the use of combination regimens and the risk of developing resistance to the beta-lactam component.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of aminoglyphoside/beta-lacatam combinations in clinical settings.
the use of antibiotics in the treatment of infections in the intensive care unit.
the development of new antibiotics, the use of antibiotics and the development of bacterial resistance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the absence of a clear-cut clinical indication for the use of an aminoside, the combination of an aminocid with a beta-lactams is not recommended.
, in the absence of a clear benefit, the combination of aminoglysides and beta-lactams should not be routinely used.
there is no evidence that combination treatment with aminogly-cosides and broad-spectrum beta- lactams has a role to play in the treatment of bacteraemia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
aminogly-cosides have a role in the treatment of serious infections, especially those caused by Gram-negative bacteria.
the combination of an aminolycoside and a beta-lactan should be used only when aminogly-cosides are indicated, and not as a standard treatment.

aminogly-cosides are still a valuable part of our antimicrobial arsenal but should be used with care and only in combination with a beta-lactamic drug when the resistance of the pathogen to beta-lactams is high enough to justify this approach.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a combination of aminogli-cosides and beta-lactams is not necessary in clinical practice.
aminoglycides should be used in combination with a beta-lactams only in the case of documented infections due to organisms known or suspected to be resistant to beta-lactam monotherapy.
, if we are to continue using aminoglyosides, they should be used as a single agent, not in combination with beta-lactams.
